Writing an operator in R

Source: vignettes/operators.Rmd
operators.Rmd

An operator is a program that runs in the cluster and looks after a kind of resource you define. You add a custom resource type (say, Site), people create Site objects, and the operator makes the cluster match what each one asks for: it creates Deployments, ConfigMaps, DNS records, whatever a site needs, and fixes them when they drift.

This guide builds one with rk8s, from an empty directory to two replicas running in a kind cluster. None of the code runs when the guide is built; it needs a cluster and Docker.

The idea: reconcile

The core of an operator is a single function. rk8s calls it with the name of an object that may need attention, and the function reads the object, works out what should exist, and makes it so. It doesn’t get told what changed, only which object to look at, so it has to work from the current state every time. That makes it safe to call as often as you like, which is what lets the rest of the machinery be simple.

rk8s calls it when the object is created, changed or deleted, when one of the objects it created changes, and after any delay you ask for. If the function fails, it’s retried with backoff.

Scaffolding

use_operator() writes a working operator to start from:

library(rk8s)
use_operator("site-operator", name = "site-operator",
             group = "example.com", kind = "Site")
site-operator/
  operator.R              the controller
  Dockerfile              builds the image
  deploy/crd.yaml         the Site resource type
  deploy/rbac.yaml        what the operator may touch
  deploy/deployment.yaml  how it runs in the cluster

The generated controller keeps, for each Site, a ConfigMap holding the site’s spec. That’s not useful on its own, but it exercises every part of the machinery, and you replace it with your own logic.

The controller

Here is operator.R, a little shortened:

library(rk8s)

k <- if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST"))) {
  kube(client = ApiClient$new(load_incluster_config()))   # running in a pod
} else {
  kube()                                                   # local development
}

reconcile <- function(req, k) {
  obj <- tryCatch(
    kube_get(k, "example.com/v1:Site", req$name, namespace = req$namespace),
    rk8s_api_error = function(e) {
      if (e$exception$status == 404L) NULL else stop(e)
    })
  if (is.null(obj)) return(NULL)

  spec <- as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(obj$spec, auto_unbox = TRUE))
  config <- list(
    apiVersion = "v1", kind = "ConfigMap",
    metadata = list(name = paste0(req$name, "-spec")),
    data = list(spec = spec))
  kube_apply(k, set_owner(config, obj), force = TRUE)

  if (!identical(obj$status$observedGeneration, obj$metadata$generation)) {
    kube_patch_status(k, obj, list(observedGeneration = obj$metadata$generation))
    kube_event(k, obj, "Reconciled", paste("updated ConfigMap", config$metadata$name))
  }
  NULL
}

mgr <- Manager$new(k)
mgr$controller("example.com/v1:Site", owns = "configmaps", reconcile = reconcile)
mgr$run(leader_election = "site-operator", health_port = 8081L)

Going through it:

  • req has the object’s namespace and name (and key, the two joined with a slash). If the object is gone, there’s usually nothing to do; see Cleaning up for when there is.
  • kube_apply() does a server-side apply, so applying the same ConfigMap again changes nothing. Write the reconcile as “this is what should exist” and apply it every time, rather than checking first.
  • set_owner() marks the ConfigMap as belonging to the Site. Two things follow. Kubernetes deletes the ConfigMap when the Site is deleted. And because the controller owns = "configmaps", any change to that ConfigMap, including someone editing it by hand, reconciles the Site, which puts the ConfigMap back.
  • kube_patch_status() writes to the object’s status, which is how an operator reports back. observedGeneration is the common convention for “I have seen this version of the spec”.
  • kube_event() records an event that shows up in kubectl describe site.
  • Returning NULL means the object is in the state it should be.

The return value controls what happens next:

Return Meaning
NULL Done until something changes
requeue() Not ready yet; try again soon, backing off each time
requeue_after(300) Look again in five minutes (for things outside the cluster)
an error Logged and retried with backoff

Running it locally

While you’re writing the reconcile, run it on your machine against a test cluster. kind works well:

kind create cluster
cd site-operator
kubectl apply -f deploy/crd.yaml
Rscript operator.R

In another terminal, create a Site:

kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: Site
metadata: {name: blog}
spec: {domain: blog.example.com, replicas: 2}
EOF

kubectl get configmap blog-spec -o jsonpath='{.data.spec}'
#> {"domain":"blog.example.com","replicas":2}
kubectl get site blog -o jsonpath='{.status}'
#> {"observedGeneration":1}

Change the spec with kubectl edit site blog and the ConfigMap follows. Delete the site and the ConfigMap goes with it.

You can also drive the manager step by step from an R session, which is handy for debugging a reconcile:

mgr$start()
mgr$step(1)    # one pass: handle what has changed, run reconciles
mgr$close()

Deploying it

Build the image, make it available to the cluster, and apply the manifests:

docker build -t site-operator:dev .
kind load docker-image site-operator:dev
kubectl apply -f deploy/
kubectl rollout status deploy/site-operator

With a registry instead of kind, push the image and set image in deploy/deployment.yaml (or pass image = to use_operator()).

The operator runs as the site-operator ServiceAccount. rbac.yaml lets it read and update Site objects and their status, manage ConfigMaps, record events, and hold its leader Lease. When your reconcile touches other resources, add them there; a missing permission shows up as a 403 in the operator’s log.

Replicas, leader election and health

Run more than one replica (replicas = 2 in use_operator(), or edit the Deployment) and only one does any work. leader_election makes the replicas compete for a Lease, and only the holder reconciles. If the leader stops renewing, another takes over within the lease duration (15 seconds by default). In a kind cluster, killing the leader pod moved the work to the standby in about 16 seconds.

health_port serves two endpoints that the generated Deployment probes:

  • /healthz answers while the manager’s loop is running. If a reconcile hangs, nothing answers, and Kubernetes restarts the pod.
  • /readyz answers once the manager is running, or standing by for the lease.

The Dockerfile starts R through tini. Without it R would be process 1 in the container, and process 1 ignores SIGTERM, so every pod deletion would wait out the full 30-second grace period before the standby could take over.

Cleaning up

Owner references handle anything inside the cluster. For things outside it, such as a DNS record or a bucket, add a finalizer. Kubernetes then keeps a deleted object around, with metadata$deletionTimestamp set, until your operator removes the finalizer:

reconcile <- function(req, k) {
  site <- tryCatch(
    kube_get(k, "example.com/v1:Site", req$name, namespace = req$namespace),
    rk8s_api_error = function(e) {
      if (e$exception$status == 404L) NULL else stop(e)
    })
  if (is.null(site)) return(NULL)

  if (is_deleting(site)) {
    delete_dns_record(site$spec$domain)        # your cleanup
    remove_finalizer(k, site, "example.com/dns")
    return(NULL)
  }
  site <- add_finalizer(k, site, "example.com/dns")
  ensure_dns_record(site$spec$domain)          # your normal work
  NULL
}

add_finalizer() does nothing if the finalizer is already there. Both it and remove_finalizer() fail with a conflict if the object changed since you read it, and the manager simply retries with fresh data.

Things to keep in mind

  • By default reconciles run one at a time, so a slow one holds up the others. Keep them short, push slow waiting into requeue_after(), or run several at once with workers (next section).
  • Write reconciles to be repeatable. They run after restarts, failovers and resyncs, and may see the same state many times.
  • The operator authenticates in the cluster with its ServiceAccount token. When developing locally with a kubeconfig, it uses whatever your kubectl uses.
  • One Manager can run several controllers; call mgr$controller() once for each resource type.

Running reconciles in parallel

If each reconcile spends time waiting, on an API outside the cluster for example, let several run at once:

mgr$controller("example.com/v1:Site", owns = "configmaps",
               reconcile = reconcile, workers = 4)

The reconciles then run in four background R processes (this needs the mirai package), while the manager keeps handling events and health checks. One Site is still never reconciled twice at the same time; a change that arrives while it is being reconciled leads to one more reconcile afterwards.

Each worker is a separate R process with its own session, built from the manager’s connection settings. Packages you attached with library() are attached there too, and so are the helper functions and values the reconcile uses from your script. What workers don’t share is state: assigning to a variable with <<- inside a reconcile changes the worker’s copy, not the manager’s. Keep anything that must be shared in the cluster, where it belongs anyway, for example in the object’s status.
